newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Bahrain stock exchange plans to open to foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Bahrain stock exchange plans to open to foreigners.

text.p: Bahrain is planning to remove restrictions blocking further foreign investment in its stock exchange to lure more funds from abroad, the stock exchange's former director said.

"After allowing foreign investors to invest in our exchange after residing for one year in any GCC country, we are now literally at the point of abolishing this condition," Fawzi Behzad told the June edition of Gulf Business magazine.
"I expect that within two months all foreign investors will be allowed to invest in the Bahrain Stock Exchange. I am expecting an emiri decree to this effect in the near future."
At the time of the Gulf Business interview Behzad was BSE director. On Monday BSE officials said he had been replaced last week by Sheikh Ahmed bin Mohammed al-Khalifa as acting director.

"Present regulations allow up to a 25 percent GCC shareholding and 24 percent foreign shareholding in the stock of companies listed on Bahrain Stock Exchange. I seek a common ceiling of 49 percent shareholding for GCC and foreign investors," he said.
The GCC -- Saudi Arabia, United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Oman, Bahrain and Qatar -- is an economic and political alliance.
Some Gulf states have said they would eventually open their bourses to foreigners. But economists have said Gulf markets are hampered by illiquidity and poor regulation.
"The advantages of foreign investment flows by far exceed their disadvantages because they add higher liquidity, depth, volume and international status," Behzad said.
He said the BSE was trying to improve transparency "by encouraging quick and regular publication of financial results".

"So far, only banks were compelled to publish quarterly results, while other listed companies were publishing their accounts on an annual basis and, in practice, sometimes three to four months later than the end of the financial year.
"This year, however a new comprehensive resolution will soon compel non-banking companies to publish their results every six months," Behzad said.

He said the bourse was considering the listing of 10 new investment funds with a capital of more than $700 million. These include a $100 million Islamic fund, a $70 million Egyptian fund and seven U.S. funds capitalised at over $400 million.
